passages.t: The people who came home, by family and by town
passages.happening:
‘Now these are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king’ (verse 1). They return to Jerusalem and Judah, ‘each to his own town’ (verse 1).

Eleven leaders are named, with Zerubbabel and Jeshua first (verse 2). Then the men of Israel are counted. First they are listed by family: the descendants of Parosh, 2,172; the descendants of Shephatiah, 372; the descendants of Arah, 775; and on through the list (verses 3-20). Then they are listed by town: ‘the men of Bethlehem, 123’ (verse 21), and after them the men of Anathoth, of Ramah and Geba, of Michmash, of Bethel and Ai, of Jericho, and others (verses 22-35).
passages.hearers:
The chapter probably records not one caravan but the people who came home in the early years of Persian rule, gathered into one register.

Its leaders matter. Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19 gives the family a little differently), so the line of David was coming home. Jeshua was the grandson of Seraiah, the last chief priest before the exile. Together they stand for the house of David and the priesthood. The Nehemiah and the Mordecai named in verse 2 are not the later governor or the cousin of Esther; these were common names.

Judah was now ‘the province’ (verse 1), a small district of the Persian empire, and the list is the kind of register such a province kept. But it also answers a question every reader had been asking since Jerusalem fell: was there still an Israel? The list's answer is yes. Here are the families, and here are the towns.

The towns named lie mostly in the old lands of Judah and Benjamin, near Jerusalem. A family's place was tied to its town and its land, and its right to that land depended on knowing who its fathers were. The people are counted first by where they belong.
passages.later:
The same list appears again in Nehemiah 7, nearly a century later, where Nehemiah says, ‘I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned’ (Nehemiah 7:5). He used it to fill Jerusalem with people again. The two copies differ in some names and figures; Nehemiah 7:7 names twelve leaders where Ezra names eleven.

Anathoth, one of the towns on the list, was Jeremiah's town: ‘Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests in Anathoth’ (Jeremiah 1:1). His was the word that Cyrus's decree fulfilled (1:1).

And Zerubbabel's name runs on into the New Testament. Matthew's family line of Jesus includes ‘Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel’ (Matthew 1:12).
passages.asks: Every family on this list had a name and a number, and a town to go back to. Ask what it means to you that God's people are counted one by one, not as a crowd. And ask whose names you have forgotten, among the people who make up the church you belong to.

passages.t: Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants
passages.happening:
Next come the people who would serve at the house of God. There are four families of priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, of Immer, of Pashhur and of Harim, more than four thousand men in all (verses 36-39). There are seventy-four Levites (verse 40). ‘The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128’ (verse 41). There are gatekeepers from six families, 139 in all (verse 42).

Then come the temple servants, family after family (verses 43-54), and the descendants of Solomon's servants (verses 55-57). ‘The temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon numbered 392 in all’ (verse 58).
passages.hearers:
The list shows how the temple community was arranged. Priests offered the sacrifices. Levites assisted them. The singers, descended from Asaph, led the worship. The gatekeepers guarded the sanctuary.

The temple servants are called in Hebrew netinim, those given: people given to the temple for its service. With the descendants of Solomon's servants, they did the heavy work around the house of God. Some of their names are not Israelite in form, and many scholars think they descended from foreigners attached to the temple long before. Their place on the roll is worth noticing. They came home, they are named by family, and they belong to the returning people.

Notice also how few Levites came. There are seventy-four of them against more than four thousand priests. When Ezra gathers a second company many years later, he will find no Levites among them at all (8:15).
passages.later:
David had set the singers in their places: ‘David and the commanders of the army set apart some of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals’ (1 Chronicles 25:1). Twelve psalms carry Asaph's name in their headings, Psalms 50 and 73 to 83, among them this one: ‘A Psalm of Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel’ (Psalm 73:1).

The temple servants turn up again when Jerusalem's wall is rebuilt: ‘the temple servants living on the hill of Ophel made repairs opposite the Water Gate’ (Nehemiah 3:26). Ezra later says that David and his officials had first appointed them to assist the Levites (8:20).
passages.asks: The singers and the gatekeepers and the temple servants are counted beside the priests. Ask whose work in your church is quiet, heavy and unseen. And ask what it would mean to honor it as this list does, by name.

passages.t: Families without records, the totals, and the gifts
passages.happening:
Some who came up could not prove ‘that their families were descended from Israel’ (verse 59). They are listed anyway, 652 of them (verse 60).

Some priests had the same trouble. ‘These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean’ (verse 62). The governor orders them not to eat the most holy things ‘until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim’ (verse 63).

‘The whole assembly numbered 42,360’ (verse 64), besides 7,337 servants and 200 singers, with their horses, mules, camels and donkeys (verses 65-67). When they arrive at the house of the LORD, some of the family heads give freewill offerings ‘to rebuild the house of God on its original site’ (verse 68). ‘According to their ability’ (verse 69), they give gold and silver and a hundred priestly garments. Then everyone settles in their towns (verse 70).
passages.hearers:
In this community, family records mattered a great deal. A family's right to land, and a priest's right to serve at the altar, depended on proof of descent. That is why the chapter pauses over those who could not show their records.

The laymen without proof are still counted. And the priests without records are not rejected as frauds. They are kept from the most holy things, the portions of the sacrifices reserved for priests, until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim. These were the sacred lots kept in the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:30), used to seek God's decision. The question is left open for God to settle. There is no record of their use after the early days of the kings, and whether such a priest ever arose, the Bible does not say.

The governor here is called by a Persian title, tirshatha, the same word later used of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 8:9).

The gold is counted in darics, a Persian gold coin usually thought to have been introduced under Darius I. If so, this sum was recorded, or put into familiar terms, some years after the first return. The gifts were given freely, each family as it could.
passages.later:
The rule that a priest must prove his descent from Aaron stands behind the argument of Hebrews 7, which notes that Jesus came from Judah, ‘a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests’ (Hebrews 7:14).

The last verse of this chapter comes back at the end of the list in Nehemiah: ‘So the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, and temple servants, along with some of the people and the rest of the Israelites, settled in their own towns’ (Nehemiah 7:73). The repetition ties the two books together.
passages.hard:
Why do the numbers not add up to 42,360, and why do they differ from Nehemiah 7?

The difficulty is real. The figures listed in Ezra 2 add up to 29,818, and those in Nehemiah 7 to 31,089, yet both lists give 42,360 as the total. About half of the separate entries differ between the two lists, usually by small amounts.

Several explanations are offered. Many scholars think the numbers were damaged in copying. Hebrew numbers in ancient manuscripts were easy to misread, and the two lists were copied separately for centuries. Others suggest that the total includes people who are not listed one by one, such as returnees from tribes other than Judah and Benjamin, or women, or those without proof of descent. Some argue that one list records those who signed up to go and the other those who arrived, with changes along the way.

None of these solutions is certain, and many interpreters combine them. The two lists agree on the shape of the list, the families and the total, and that agreement is what the lists were meant to keep: the record of a people restored.
passages.asks: Those without records were not sent away. They were asked to wait until God could decide. Ask how you handle uncertainty about who belongs, in a church or in your own sense of belonging. And ask what you give, as these families gave, according to your ability.
